title: Attention Residue
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: DistillED translates Sophie Leroy's 2009 organizational-behavior research on attention residue, the persistence of cognitive activity on an unfinished task even after a person has moved on, into a classroom transition strategy. The newsletter is careful to separate what Leroy's lab experiments actually showed from what it is extrapolating for teachers: her key finding was that simply finishing a task did not clear residue, but finishing under a felt deadline did, because it produced the confidence that the goal had genuinely been met. From that mechanism, the piece builds a five-step "Create Clear Time Boundaries" sequence (set the time, make it visible, cue time remaining, allow for closure, signal the shift) designed to give students an experienced, not merely announced, endpoint to a task before the next one begins. The larger argument is that a transition in classroom activity does not automatically produce a transition in student attention, and closure is something a lesson has to be built to deliver rather than assume.
points: The newsletter explicitly flags where Leroy's actual lab findings end and its own classroom extrapolation begins, distinguishing a research summary from a teaching-practice inference rather than blurring the two.

The counterintuitive finding is that finishing a task calmly does not clear attention residue; only finishing under a felt deadline did, because time pressure produced the confidence that the goal was actually met, not completion itself.

The five-step sequence deliberately pairs a countdown with a 'last move' step, arguing that visible urgency without a concrete stopping point reproduces the unhurried-finish condition Leroy's data shows still leaves residue behind.

The core reframe for teachers is that a task doesn't end for a student's attention just because a teacher announces it's over; closure has to be experienced through the structure of the transition, not simply declared.
quotes: Attention residue reflects the persistence of cognitive activity about a Task A even though one stopped working on Task A and currently performs a Task B.

Performance also suffers when people have completed a prior task under low time pressure. It is only when people have completed the prior task under high time pressure that their subsequent task performance is enhanced.
For teachers, the takeaway isn't just add a timer. It's a bit narrower and more useful than that: a task doesn't end for a student's attention just because you've announced it's over.
An unannounced stop catches attention mid-task, which is exactly the unfinished state Leroy's data associates with residue. Staged warnings give students time to start wrapping up before the switch.
A small, definite last move, reached while time is genuinely tight, is closer to her high-pressure completion condition than to an unhurried finish.

The point worth holding onto is the mechanism, not the exact wording: a transition in activity doesn't guarantee a transition in attention, and the more predictable and closed you make the boundary, the less of Task A a student is likely to be carrying into Task B.
